t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q: But wherefore doth He set forth this parable in the person of the virgins, and doth not merely suppose any person whatever? Great things had He spoken of virginity, saying, "There are eunuchs, who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of Heaven's sake;" and, "He that is able to receive, let him receive it." He knew also that the generality of men would have a great opinion of it. For indeed the work is by nature great, and is shown so by this, that neither under the old dispensation was it fulfilled by these ancient and holy men, nor under the new was it brought under the compulsion of the law. For He did not command this, but left it to the choice of his hearers. Wherefore Paul also said "Now, concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord." "For though I praise him that attains thereto, yet I constrain not him that is not willing, neither do I make the thing an injunction." Since then the thing is both great in itself and hath great honor with the multitude, lest any one attaining to this should feel as though he had attained to all, and should be careless about the rest, He putteth forth this parable sufficient to persuade them, that virginity, though it should have everything else, if destitute of the good things arising out of almsgiving, is cast out with the harlots, and He sets the inhuman and merciless with them. And most reasonably, for the one was overcome by the love of carnal pleasure, but these of money. But the love of carnal pleasure and of money are not equal, but that of carnal pleasure is far keener and more tyrannical. And the weaker the antagonist, the less excusable are these that are overcome thereby. Therefore also He calls them foolish, for that having undergone the greater labor, they have betrayed all for want of the less. But by lamps here, He meaneth the gift itself of virginity, the purity of holiness; and by oil, humanity, almsgiving, succor to them that are in need.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
These parables are like the former parable of the faithful servant, and of him that was ungrateful and devoured his Lord's goods. For there are four in all, in different ways admonishing us about the same things, I mean about diligence in almsgiving, and about helping our neighbor by all means which we are able to use, since it is not possible to be saved in another way. But there He speaks more generally of all assistance which should be rendered to one's neighbor; but as to the virgins, he speaketh particularly of mercifulness in alms, and more strongly than in the former parable. For there He punishes him that beats, and is drunken, and scatters and wastes his lord's goods, but here even him that doth not help, nor spends abundantly his goods upon the needy. For they had oil indeed, but not in abundance, wherefore also they are punished.

But wherefore doth He set forth this parable in the person of the virgins, and doth not merely suppose any person whatever? Great things had He spoken of virginity, saying, "There are eunuchs, who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of Heaven's sake;" and, "He that is able to receive, let him receive it." He knew also that the generality of men would have a great opinion of it. For indeed the work is by nature great, and is shown so by this, that neither under the old dispensation was it fulfilled by these ancient and holy men, nor under the new was it brought under the compulsion of the law. For He did not command this, but left it to the choice of his hearers. Wherefore Paul also said "Now, concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord." "For though I praise him that attains thereto, yet I constrain not him that is not willing, neither do I make the thing an injunction." Since then the thing is both great in itself and hath great honor with the multitude, lest any one attaining to this should feel as though he had attained to all, and should be careless about the rest, He putteth forth this parable sufficient to persuade them, that virginity, though it should have everything else, if destitute of the good things arising out of almsgiving, is cast out with the harlots, and He sets the inhuman and merciless with them. And most reasonably, for the one was overcome by the love of carnal pleasure, but these of money. But the love of carnal pleasure and of money are not equal, but that of carnal pleasure is far keener and more tyrannical. And the weaker the antagonist, the less excusable are these that are overcome thereby. Therefore also He calls them foolish, for that having undergone the greater labor, they have betrayed all for want of the less. But by lamps here, He meaneth the gift itself of virginity, the purity of holiness; and by oil, humanity, almsgiving, succor to them that are in need.

"Then, while the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept." He shows that the time intervening will not be short, leading His disciples away from the expectation that His kingdom was quite immediately to appear. For this indeed they hoped, therefore He is continually holding them back from this hope. And at the same time He intimates this too, that death is a sleep. For they slept, He saith.

"And about midnight there was a cry made." Either He was continuing the parable, or again He shows that the resurrection will be at night. But the cry Paul also indicates, saying, "With a shout, with a voice of an archangel, with the last trump, He shall come down from Heaven." And what mean the trumpets, and what saith the cry? "The bridegroom cometh." When therefore they had trimmed their lamps, the foolish say unto the wise, "Give us of your oil." Again He calls them foolish, showing that nothing can be more foolish than they who are wealthy here, and depart naked thither, where most of all we have need of humanity, where we want much oil. But not in this respect only were they foolish, but also because they looked to receive it there, and sought it out of season; and yet nothing could be more humane than those virgins, who for this especially were approved. Neither do they seek for it all, for, "Give us," they say, "of your oil;" and the urgency of their need is indicated; "for our lamps," they say, "are going out." But even so they failed, and neither the humanity of those whom they asked, nor the easiness of their request, nor their necessity and want, made them obtain.

But what now do we learn from hence? That no man can protect us there, if we are betrayed by our works, not because he will not, but because he cannot. For these too take refuge in the impossibility. This the blessed Abraham also indicated, saying, "Between us and you there is a great gulf," so that not even when willing is it permitted them to pass it.

"But go to them that sell, and buy." And who are they that sell? The poor. And where are these? Here, and then should they have sought them, not at that time.

Seest thou what great profit arises to us from the poor? shouldest thou take them away, thou wouldest take away the great hope of our salvation. Wherefore here must we get together the oil, that it may be useful to us there, when the time calls us. For that is not the time of collecting it, but this. Spend not then your goods for nought in luxury and vainglory. For thou wilt have need of much oil there.

Having heard these things, those virgins went their way; but they profited nothing. And this He saith, either pursuing the parable, and working it up; or also by these things showing, that though we should become humane after our departure, we shall gain nothing from thence towards our escape. Therefore neither did their forwardness avail these virgins, because they went to them that sell not here, but there; nor the rich man, when he became so charitable, as even to be anxious about his relations. For he that was passing by him that was laid at the gate, is eager to rescue from perils and from hell them whom he did not so much as see, and entreats that some be sent to tell them these things. But nevertheless, he derived no benefit from thence, as neither did these virgins. For when they having heard these things went their way, the bridegroom came, and they that were ready went in with Him, but the others were shut out. After their many labors, after their innumerable toils, and that intolerable fight, and those trophies which they had set up over the madness of natural appetite, disgraced, and with their lamps gone out, they withdrew, bending down their faces to the earth. For nothing is more sullied than virginity not having mercy; so that even the multitude are wont to call the unmerciful dark. Where then was the profit of virginity, when they saw not the bridegroom? and not even when they had knocked did they obtain, but they heard that fearful saying, "Depart, I know you not." And when He hath said this, nothing else but hell is left, and that intolerable punishment; or rather, this word is more grievous even than hell. This word He speaks to them also that work iniquity.

"Watch therefore, for ye know not the day nor the hour." Seest thou how continually He adds this, showing how awful our ignorance concerning our departure hence? Where now are they, who throughout all their life are remiss, but when they are blamed by us, are saying, At the time of my death, I shall leave money to the poor. Let them listen to these words, and be amended. For indeed at that time many have failed of this, having been snatched away at once, and not permitted so much as to give charge to their relations touching what they wished to be done.
(Lib. 83 Quæst. q. 59.) Or, The lamps which they carry in their hands are their works, of which it was said above, Let your works shine before men. (Mat. 5:16.)

(ubi sup.) Or, that the virgins go forth to meet the bridegroom alone, I think is to be understood that the virgins themselves constitute her who is called the bride; as we speak of the Christians flocking to the Church as children running to their mother, and yet this same mother consists only of the children who are gathered together. For now the Church is betrothed, and is to be led forth as a virgin to the marriage, which takes place then when all her mortal part having past away, she may be held in an eternal union.

(Ep. 199. 45.) There have not been wanting those who would refer these ten virgins to that coming of Christ, which takes place now in the Church; but this is not to be hastily held out, lest any thing should occur contradictory of it.

(Hom. in Ev. xii. 1.) By the kingdom of heaven is meant the present Church, as in that, The Son of Man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend. (Matt. 13:41.)

(ubi sup.) For in each of the five senses of the body there is a double instrument, and the number five doubled makes ten. And because the company of the faithful is gathered out of both sexes, the Holy Church is described as being like to ten virgins, where as bad are mixed with good, and reprobate with elect, it is like a mixture of wise and foolish virgins.
Then, because all this discourse is concerning the great day of the Lord, concerning which He had been speaking before.
Or, The bridegroom and the bride represent our Lord God in the body, for the flesh is the bride of the spirit. The lamps are the light of bright souls which shine forth in the sacrament of baptismb.

This parable of the ten foolish and the ten wise virgins, some interpret literally of virgins, of whom there are according to the Apostle some who are virgins both in body and in thought, (1 Cor. 7.) others who have preserved indeed their bodies virgin, but have not the other deeds of virgins, or have only been preserved by the guardianship of parents, but have wedded in their hearts. But from what has gone before, I think the meaning to be different, and that the parable has reference not to virgins only, but to the whole human race.

Then the kingdom of heaven shall be like ten virgins, who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. But five of them were foolish and five prudent.

In all who have learned the word of God, the kingdom of heaven is likened to ten virgins. And if indeed in those who both rightly believe and rightly live and therefore …, it is justly likened to the five prudent ones, while those who indeed profess faith in Jesus but do not prepare themselves by good works for salvation are likened to the remaining five foolish virgins, we say not without reason that the senses of all who have learned divine things — in whatever way they have received the word of God, "whether by occasion or in truth" — are virgins made virgin through the word of God in which they have believed or wish to believe. For such is the word of God that it imparts of its own purity to all who through its teaching have indeed withdrawn from the worship of idols or the worship of the elements of God's creation, but have come through Jesus Christ to the worship of God, even though works of piety have not followed nor have they prepared themselves for blessedness.

But just as, according to the word of truth, the virtues follow one after another — which virtues are in substance Christ —

so that whoever has one has them all, and whoever lacks one does not have even one (for Christ is inseparable from himself), so also all the senses follow one after another; and wherever one of the senses falls short according to the right teaching of the word, there all the senses too, as if defrauded of the word of wisdom, are made foolish.

Now by "senses" I mean both those which are commonly understood — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch — and those which in the Proverbs are called divine,

by those who speak in this manner: "You will find a divine sense". But again, since the word of God is the cause that the use of the senses becomes right, and since it is not possible that it, being in the senses, … that it should indeed work in certain senses and diligently bestow the things that belong to its own prudence, but in others neglect them — therefore, if it has made one of the senses wise, so that it may be constituted a virgin, it is necessary that it pour out its wisdom in the other senses as well.

For this reason it is not possible to see, among the five senses in anyone, some indeed foolish and others prudent; but it is necessary that either all five be prudent, or all foolish.

All these senses take their lamps, that is, their natural organs, whether wishing to use them according to the word of God, or even against the will of God; nevertheless they take them, when they accept that the word of God and Son of God is the bridegroom of the Church; and they go out from the world and from the errors of the many gods, and they come to meet the Savior, who is always ready to come to those virgins,

so that he may enter together with the worthy among them to the blessed bride, the Church. But so long as, after the word has been received, the light of the faithful shines "before men, that seeing their good works they may glorify their Father who is in heaven", these are both prudent and receive oil — the nourishment of the light, which is always poured into good acts, that is, the word of teaching,

and, filling the vessels of their souls from this word — from the teachers and transmitters who sell it — with what may be enough for them even if the departure delays and the word coming to their consummation tarries, so that, being consummated and made outside the world, they may hasten thither. But those who had no care, after the beginning of Christianity, to receive so great a teaching of the word as would suffice for them to endure until the end, being negligent about the reception of the teaching which strengthens faith and illuminates the light of good acts (and what strengthens so much as moral discourse, which is called the oil of the light?) — these are foolish, and they received lamps at first indeed lit, but for so great a journey of going out to meet the bridegroom they received no oil. And while the bridegroom tarried, all the virgins slumbered and slept. So, while the bridegroom tarries and the word does not come quickly to the consummation of their life, from this they suffer something as it were of the senses, and act and slumber as it were in the night of the world. They slept indeed (that is, they acted more slackly with respect to that vital sense), yet those prudent ones neither lost their lamps nor despaired of preserving the oil.

Or, The understandings of all who have received the word of God are virgins. For such is the word of God, that of its purity it imparts to all, who by its teaching have departed from the worship of idols, and have through Christ drawn near to the worship of God; Which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom and the bridea. They take their lamps, i. e. their natural faculties, and go forth out of the world and its errors, and go to meet the Saviour, who is ever ready to come to enter with them that are worthy to His blessed bride the Church.

(ubi sup.) Or, by the five virgins, is denoted a five-fold continence from the allurements of the flesh; for our appetite must be held from gratification of the eyes, ears, smell, taste, and touch. And as this continence may be done before God, to please Him in inward joy of the conscience, or before men only to gain applause of men, five are called wise, and five foolish. Both are virgins, because both these men exercise continence, though from different motives.
Or, The five wise and five foolish are an absolute distinction between believers and unbelievers.

For there are five senses which hasten towards heavenly things, and seek after things above. Of sight, hearing, and touch, it is specially said, That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have handled. (1 John 1:1.) Of taste, Taste and see that the Lord is good. (Ps. 34:8.) Of smell, Because of the savour of thy good ointments. (Sol. Song, 1:3.) There are also other five senses which gape after earthly husks.

They that believe rightly, and live righteously, are likened to the five wise; they that profess the faith of Jesus, but prepare themselves not by good works to salvation, are likened to the five foolish.

And because the virtues are so linked together, that he who has one has all, so all the senses so follow one another, that all must be wise, or all foolish.

(ubi sup.) Or, The oil denotes joy, according to that, God hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness. (Ps. 45:7.) He then whose joy springs not from this that he is inwardly pleasing to God, has no oil with him; for they have no gladness in their continent lives, save in the praises of men. But the wise took oil with their lamps, that is, the gladness of good works, in their vessels, that is, they stored it in their heart and conscience, as the Apostle speaks, Let every man prove himself, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself, and not in another. (Gal. 6:4.)
(Hom. in Ev. xii. 1.) It is to be observed, that all have lamps, but all have not oil.
The oil is the fruit of good works, the vessels are the human bodies in whose inward parts the treasure of a good conscience is to be laid up.
The virgins that have oil are they who, besides their faith, have the ornament of good works; they that have not oil, are they that seem to confess with like faith, but neglect the works of virtue.

Or, The oil is the word of teaching, with which the vessels of souls are filled; for what gives so great content as moral discourse, which is called the oil of light. The wise took with them of this oil, as much as would suffice, though the Word should tarry long, and be slack to come to their consummation. The foolish took lamps, alight indeed at the first, but not supplied with so much oil as should suffice even to the end, being careless respecting the provision of doctrine which comforts faith, and enlightens the lamp of good deeds.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q: "Then, while the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept." He shows that the time intervening will not be short, leading His disciples away from the expectation that His kingdom was quite immediately to appear. For this indeed they hoped, therefore He is continually holding them back from this hope. And at the same time He intimates this too, that death is a sleep. For they slept, He saith.
(ubi sup.) For there die of both kinds of men in this interval of time before the resurrection of the dead, and the Lord's coming shall be.
(Hom. in Ev. xii. 1.) To sleep is to die, to slumber before sleep is to faint from salvation before death, because, by the burden of sickness we come to the sleep of death.

Or, They slumbered, i. e. they were dead. And then follows, And slept, because they were to be afterwards wakened. While the bridegroom tarried, shows that no little time intervened between the Lord's first and second coming.

Or, Whilst the bridegroom tarried, and the Word comes not speedily to the consummation of this life, the senses suffer, slumbering and moving in the night of the world; and sleep, as energizing feebly, and with no quick sense. Yet did those wise virgins not quit their lamps, nor despair of hoarding their oil.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q: "And about midnight there was a cry made." Either He was continuing the parable, or again He shows that the resurrection will be at night. But the cry Paul also indicates, saying, "With a shout, with a voice of an archangel, with the last trump, He shall come down from Heaven." And what mean the trumpets, and what saith the cry? "The bridegroom cometh."
(ubi sup.) Or, At midnight, that is, when none knew or looked for it.
At the trumpet signal they go forth to meet the bridegroom alone, for then shall the two be one, that is, the flesh and God, when the lowliness of the flesh shall be transformed into spiritual glory.

The Jews have a tradition that Christ will come at midnight, in like manner as in that visitation of Egypt, when the Paschal feast is celebrated, and the destroyer comes, and the Lord passes over our dwellings, and the door posts of each man's countenance are hallowed by the blood of the Lamb. Hence, I suppose, has continued among us that apostolic tradition, that on the vigil of Easter the people should not be dismissed before midnight, in expectation of Christ's coming; but when that hour has past over, they may celebrate the feast in security; whence also the Psalmist says, At midnight did I rise to praise thee. (Ps. 119:62.)

Suddenly thus, as on a stormy night, and when all think themselves secure, at the hour when sleep is the deepest, the coming of Christ shall be proclaimed by the shout of Angels, and the trumpets of the Powers that go before Him. This is meant when it says, Lo, the bridegroom cometh, go ye out to meet him.

But at midnight a cry arose: behold, the bridegroom comes, rise up to meet him. Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. But the foolish said to the wise: give us of your oil, for our lamps are going out. But the wise answered, saying: lest perhaps there be not enough for us and for you; go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves. But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding, and the door was shut. But afterward the rest of the virgins also came, saying: lord, lord, open to us. But he answering said: amen I say to you, I do not know you.

But at midnight, that is, in the depth of relaxation, and in the middle time, when the evening light has now passed away and the daytime light is still awaited, a cry arose from those wishing (as I think) to rouse all — the angels, who "are all ministering spirits, who are sent to minister for the sake of those who shall possess salvation", who also were anxious to rouse those who are perceptive to meet the bridegroom, and they say, crying out within in the senses of all who sleep:

behold, the bridegroom comes, rise up to meet him. And that they ought to go to meet the bridegroom, the Word, and the spotless Church, this suggestion indeed all heard, and they arose: yet not all put upon their lamps a fitting adornment, but only those who heard the wisdom that adorns them. Thus not at a suitable time the foolish said to the wise: give us of your oil, as those who had not gathered wisdom for themselves beforehand, so that they might understand that it does not belong to all who have oil also to give of it to others who wish it, but only to those who have been appointed for this very thing, that they may sell and bestow and receive the price of the oil sold, whose price is perseverance and persistence and love of learning and diligence and the labor of those who desire to learn.

give us of your oil, for our lamps are going out. For even though they were foolish, yet they understood this, that they ought to go to meet the bridegroom with light, having all the lamps of the senses illuminated. And they saw also this, that from the fact that they had less of the rational oil, now that the darkness was drawing near, their lamps were bound to be darkened. But the wise send the foolish away to the sellers of oil, seeing that they had not gathered so much oil, that is, the word of doctrine, that it might suffice both for themselves unto life and for them to teach the others to adorn their lamps. And if you consider someone at some time, who indeed has gathered the doctrine of the word to the extent that it suffices him for living well, yet not so that he can even become a teacher, you will see such a one answering those who wish to learn from him the things that are of God, and saying: lest perhaps there be not enough for us and for you: for I have the doctrine of the word sufficient for myself to live well, yet not so that I can also supply doctrine to you as well.

And they will answer those who wish to learn from them: go rather to the sellers and buy for yourselves, that is: to the teachers, and receive from them. And the foolish, going not when they ought to buy for themselves the doctrine, lose the time of entering in with the bridegroom to the wedding.

And it is possible to see those who suffer such things, who, when indeed they ought to have learned, neglected to learn anything useful from those from whom they ought to have learned,

but at the very departure of their life, while they are arranging to learn,

are seized by death, and therefore they do not enter in with the Word to the bride, the Church, nor with Christ to those who are to be together in rest and to reign in blessedness. But afterward the door is shut against the foolish virgins who are still to receive oil, who also will come afterward without cause, saying: lord, lord, open to us. And so the bridegroom answering says: I do not know you.

And so, because the parable was being spoken to all the hearers, he adds, saying to his disciples: watch therefore, for you know not the day nor the hour.

Now the lamps of the senses are adorned by evangelical and upright uses, so that there may be an adornment of the eyes in the right use of seeing, that the eyes may see so as to admire the Maker, but may be closed "so as not to see iniquity". And the hearing is an adornment when someone does not admit a vain hearing, but "stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood", and hears Jesus saying to him: "be opened", so that they may be presented only to salutary and necessary words.

Thus too concerning the adornment of taste one can speak, and of smell and of touch, according to the things that have been said, because for those who use their senses wrongly there is no adornment either in the eyes or in the ears or in the rest of the senses. But it is to be observed that it is indeed written that the foolish were sent away to procure oil, yet it is not recorded that they bought or received it, but (this being passed over in silence) it is afterward said that after this the rest of the virgins also come, saying: lord, lord, open to us. Whereas he could have said: afterward they came having received or procured oil, he fittingly kept silent, so that he might not say to those who had oil, or who at the last were adorning their lamps: I do not know who you are. For neither is it written that they came adorning their lamps.

Yet the aim of the word is this, that at every time we prepare ourselves for the departure,

so that we may not give sleep to our eyes nor slumber to our eyelids, because we know not the day and the hour of our departure.

Or, At midnight, that is, at the time of their most abandoned carelessness, there was a great cry, of the Angels, I suppose, desiring to arouse all men, those ministering spirits crying within in the senses of all that sleep, Behold, the bridegroom cometh, go ye out to meet him. All heard this summons, and arose, but all were not able to trim their lamps fitly. The lamps of the senses are trimmed by evangelical and right use of them; and they that use their senses amiss have their lamps untrimmed.
(ubi sup.) They trimmed their lamps, that is, prepared to give an account of their deeds.

(ubi sup.) From habit, the mind seeks that which uses to give it pleasure. And these now seek from men, who see not the heart, witness to God, who sees the heart. But their lamps go out, because those, whose good works rest upon the testimony of others, when that is withdrawn, sink into nothing.

(ubi sup.) Or, All the virgins arose, that is, both elect and reprobate are roused from the sleep of death; they trimmed their lamps, that is, they reckon up to themselves their works for which they look to receive eternal blessedness.
Or, the trimming their lamps is the return of their souls into their bodies, and their light is the consciousness of good works that shines forth, which is contained in the vessels of the body.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
When therefore they had trimmed their lamps, the foolish say unto the wise, "Give us of your oil." Again He calls them foolish, showing that nothing can be more foolish than they who are wealthy here, and depart naked thither, where most of all we have need of humanity, where we want much oil. But not in this respect only were they foolish, but also because they looked to receive it there, and sought it out of season; and yet nothing could be more humane than those virgins, who for this especially were approved. Neither do they seek for it all, for, "Give us," they say, "of your oil;" and the urgency of their need is indicated; "for our lamps," they say, "are going out." But even so they failed, and neither the humanity of those whom they asked, nor the easiness of their request, nor their necessity and want, made them obtain.

But what now do we learn from hence? That no man can protect us there, if we are betrayed by our works, not because he will not, but because he cannot. For these too take refuge in the impossibility. This the blessed Abraham also indicated, saying, "Between us and you there is a great gulf," so that not even when willing is it permitted them to pass it.

(ubi sup.) The lamps of the foolish virgins go out, because the works which appeared outwardly to men to be bright, are dimmed within at the coming of the Judge. That they then beg oil of the wise virgins, what is it but that at the coming of the Judge, when they find themselves empty within, they seek for witness from without? As though deceived by their own self-confidence, they say to their neighbours, Whereas ye see us rejected as living without works, do ye witness to our works that ye have seen.

Or, These virgins who complain that their lamps are gone out, show that they are partially alight, yet have they not an unfailing light, nor enduring works. Whoso then has a virgin soul, and is a lover of chastity, ought not to rest content with such virtues as quickly fade, and are withered away when the heat comes upon them, but should follow after perfect virtues, that he may have an enduring light.

Otherwise; Notwithstanding they were foolish, they yet understood that they must have light to go and meet the bridegroom, that all the lights of their senses might be burning. This also they discerned, that because they had little of the spiritual oil, their lamps would burn dim as darkness drew on. But the wise send the foolish to those that sell, seeing that they had not stored up so much oil, that is, word of doctrine, as would suffice both for themselves to live by, and to teach others, Go ye rather to them that sell, i. e. to the doctors, and buy, i. e. take of them; the price is perseverance, the love of learning, industry, and toil of all who are willing to learn.
If, however, you are a sinner, how will the oil of your puny torch be able to suffice for you and for me?

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
"But go to them that sell, and buy." And who are they that sell? The poor. And where are these? Here, and then should they have sought them, not at that time.

Seest thou what great profit arises to us from the poor? shouldest thou take them away, thou wouldest take away the great hope of our salvation. Wherefore here must we get together the oil, that it may be useful to us there, when the time calls us. For that is not the time of collecting it, but this. Spend not then your goods for nought in luxury and vainglory. For thou wilt have need of much oil there.

(ubi sup.) Or we may suppose it not meant as advice what they should do, but as an indirect allusion to their fault. For flatterers sell oil, who by praising things false, and things unknown, lead souls astray, recommending to them, as foolish, empty joys, and receiving in return some temporal benefit. Go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves, i. e. Let us now see what they can profit you who have used to sell you their praise. Lest there be not enough for us and you, because no man is profited in God's sight by the testimony of others, because God sees the heart, and each man is scarce able to give testimony concerning his own conscience.

They that sell are the poor, who, needing the alms of the faithful, made them that recompense which they desire, selling in return for the relief afforded to their wants, a consciousness of good works. This is the abundant fuel of an undying light which may be bought and stored up for the fruits of mercy.

For these wise virgins do not answer thus out of covetousness, but out of fear. Wherefore, each man shall receive the recompense of his own works, and the virtues of one cannot atone for the vices of another in the day of judgment. The wise admonish them not to go to meet the bridegroom without oil, Go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.

And this oil is sold, and at a high cost, nor is it to be got without much toil; so that we understand it not of alms only, but of all virtues and counsels of the teachers.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q: Having heard these things, those virgins went their way; but they profited nothing. And this He saith, either pursuing the parable, and working it up; or also by these things showing, that though we should become humane after our departure, we shall gain nothing from thence towards our escape. Therefore neither did their forwardness avail these virgins, because they went to them that sell not here, but there; nor the rich man, when he became so charitable, as even to be anxious about his relations. For he that was passing by him that was laid at the gate, is eager to rescue from perils and from hell them whom he did not so much as see, and entreats that some be sent to tell them these things. But nevertheless, he derived no benefit from thence, as neither did these virgins. For when they having heard these things went their way, the bridegroom came, and they that were ready went in with Him, but the others were shut out. After their many labors, after their innumerable toils, and that intolerable fight, and those trophies which they had set up over the madness of natural appetite, disgraced, and with their lamps gone out, they withdrew, bending down their faces to the earth. For nothing is more sullied than virginity not having mercy; so that even the multitude are wont to call the unmerciful dark. Where then was the profit of virginity, when they saw not the bridegroom? and not even when they had knocked did they obtain, but they heard that fearful saying, "Depart, I know you not." And when He hath said this, nothing else but hell is left, and that intolerable punishment; or rather, this word is more grievous even than hell. This word He speaks to them also that work iniquity.

(ubi sup.) Or otherwise; While they went to buy, that is, while they turned themselves to things without, and sought to find pleasure in things they had been accustomed to, because they knew not inward joys, came He that judges; and they that were ready, i. e. they whose conscience bore witness to them before God, went in with him to the wedding, i. e. to where the pure soul is united prolific to the pure and perfect word of God.

(ubi sup.) When they have been taken in who have been changed into angelic being (1 Cor. 15:51), all entrance into the kingdom of heaven is closed; after the judgment, there is no more place for prayers or merit.
The marriage is the putting on of immortality, and the joining together corruption and incorruption in a new union...

But because the season for buying was now past, and the day of judgment was coming on, so that there was no room for penitence, they must not now lay up new works, but give an account of the old.

After the day of judgment, there is no more opportunity for good works, or for righteousness, and therefore it follows, And the door was shut.

Or, He says, While they went to buy, because there are men to be found who have neglected to learn any thing useful, till when, in the very end of their life, when they set themselves to learn, they are overtaken by death.
Yet though the season of repentance is now past, the foolish virgins come and beg that entrance may be granted to them.
Their worthy confession calling Him, Lord, Lord, is a mark of faith. But what avails it to confess with the mouth Him whom you deny with your works?

(ubi sup.) It is not said that they bought any oil, and therefore we must suppose that all their delight in the praise of men being gone, they return in distress and affliction to implore God. But His severity, after judgment, is as great as His mercy was unspeakable before. But He answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not; by that rule, namely, that the art of God, that is, His wisdom, does not admit that those should enter into His joy who have sought to do in any thing according to His commandments, not as before God, but that they may please men.

For the Lord knoweth them that are his, (2 Tim. 2:19.) and he that knoweth not shall not be known, and though they be virgins in purity of body, or in confession of the true faith, yet forasmuch as they have no oil, they are unknown by the bridegroom.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
"Watch therefore, for ye know not the day nor the hour." Seest thou how continually He adds this, showing how awful our ignorance concerning our departure hence? Where now are they, who throughout all their life are remiss, but when they are blamed by us, are saying, At the time of my death, I shall leave money to the poor. Let them listen to these words, and be amended. For indeed at that time many have failed of this, having been snatched away at once, and not permitted so much as to give charge to their relations touching what they wished to be done.

This parable was spoken with respect to mercy in alms; but the one that comes after this, to them that neither in money, nor in word, nor in protection, nor in any other things whatever, are willing to assist their neighbors, but withhold all.

(ubi sup.) For indeed we know the day and the hour neither of that future time when the Bridegroom will come, nor of our own falling asleep each of us; if then we be prepared for this latter, we shall also be prepared when that voice shall sound, which shall arouse us all.

When He adds, Watch therefore, because ye know not the day nor the hour, He means that all that has been said points to this, namely, that seeing we know not the day of judgment, we should be careful in providing the light of good works.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
This parable was spoken with respect to mercy in alms; but the one that comes after this, to them that neither in money, nor in word, nor in protection, nor in any other things whatever, are willing to assist their neighbors, but withhold all.

And wherefore can it be that this parable brings forward a king, but that a bridegroom? That thou mightest learn how close Christ is joined unto the virgins that strip themselves of their possessions; for this indeed is virginity. Wherefore Paul also makes this as a definition of the thing. "The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord;" such are his words: and, "For that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction. These things we advise," he saith.

And if in Luke the parable of the talents is otherwise put, this is to be said, that the one is really different from the other. For in that, from the one capital different degrees of increase were made, for from one pound one brought five, another ten; wherefore neither did they obtain the same recompense; but here, it is the contrary, and the crown is accordingly equal. For he that received two gave two, and he that had received the five again in like manner; but there since from the same beginning one made the greater, one the less, increase; as might be expected, in the rewards also, they do not enjoy the same.

But see Him everywhere, not requiring it again immediately. For in the case of the vineyard, He let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country; and here He committed to them the talents, and took His journey, that thou mightest learn His long-suffering. And to me He seems to say these things, to intimate the resurrection. But here it is no more a vineyard and husbandmen, but all servants. For not to rulers only, nor to Jews, but to all, doth He address His discourse. And they who bring a return unto Him confess frankly, both what is their own, and what their Master's. And the one saith, Lord, "Thou gavest me five talents;" and the other saith, "two," indicating that from Him they received the source of their gain, and they are very thankful, and reckon all to Him.

What then saith the Master? "Well done, thou good" (for this is goodness to look to one's neighbor) "and faithful servant; thou wast faithful over few things, I will set thee over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy Lord," meaning by this expression all blessedness.

But not so that other one, but how? "I knew that thou art a hard man, reaping where thou sowedst not, and gathering where thou strawedst not: and I was afraid, and hid thy talent: lo, there thou hast that is thine." What then the Master? "Thou oughtest to have put my money to the exchangers," that is, "thou oughtest to have spoken, to have admonished, to have advised." But are they disobedient? Yet this is nought to thee.

What could be more gentle than this? For men indeed do not so, but him that hath put out the money at usury, even him do they make also responsible to require it again. But He not so; but, Thou oughtest, He saith, to have put it out, and to have committed the requiring of it again to me. And I should have required it with increase; by increase upon the hearing, meaning the showing forth of the works. Thou oughtest to have done that which is easier, and to have left to me what is more difficult. Forasmuch then as he did not this, "Take," saith He, "the talent from him, and give it to him that hath ten talents. For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance; but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath." What then is this? He that hath a gift of word and teaching to profit thereby, and useth it not, will lose the gift also; but he that giveth diligence, will gain to himself the gift in more abundance; even as the other loseth what he had received. But not to this is the penalty limited for him that is slothful, but even intolerable is the punishment, and with the punishment the sentence, which is full of a heavy accusation. For "cast ye," saith He, "the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Seest thou how not only the spoiler, and the covetous, nor only the doer of evil things, but also he that doeth not good things, is punished with extreme punishment.

Let us hearken then to these words. As we have opportunity, let us help on our salvation, let us get oil for our lamps, let us labor to add to our talent. For if we be backward, and spend our time in sloth here, no one will pity us any more hereafter, though we should wail ten thousand times. He also that had on the filthy garments condemned himself, and profited nothing. He also that had the one talent restored that which was committed to his charge, and yet was condemned. The virgins again entreated, and came unto Him and knocked, and all in vain, and without effect.

Knowing then these things, let us contribute alike wealth, and diligence, and protection, and all things for our neighbor's advantage. For the talents here are each person's ability, whether in the way of protection, or in money, or in teaching, or in what thing soever of the kind. Let no man say, I have but one talent, and can do nothing; for thou canst even by one approve thyself. For thou art not poorer than that widow; thou art not more uninstructed than Peter and John, who were both "unlearned and ignorant men;" but nevertheless, since they showed forth a zeal, and did all things for the common good, they attained to Heaven. For nothing is so pleasing to God, as to live for the common advantage.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
And wherefore can it be that this parable brings forward a king, but that a bridegroom? That thou mightest learn how close Christ is joined unto the virgins that strip themselves of their possessions; for this indeed is virginity. Wherefore Paul also makes this as a definition of the thing. "The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord;" such are his words: and, "For that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction. These things we advise," he saith.

And if in Luke the parable of the talents is otherwise put, this is to be said, that the one is really different from the other. For in that, from the one capital different degrees of increase were made, for from one pound one brought five, another ten; wherefore neither did they obtain the same recompense; but here, it is the contrary, and the crown is accordingly equal. For he that received two gave two, and he that had received the five again in like manner; but there since from the same beginning one made the greater, one the less, increase; as might be expected, in the rewards also, they do not enjoy the same.

(Hom. in Ev. ix, l.) The man travelling into a far country is our Redeemer, who ascended into heaven in that flesh which He had taken upon Him. For the proper home of the flesh is the earth, and it, as it were, travels into a foreign country, when it is placed by the Redeemer in heaven.

Calling together the Apostles, He gave them the Gospel doctrine, to one more, to another less, not as of His own bounty or scanting, but as meeting the capacity of the receivers, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 3:2.), that he fed with milk those that were unable to take solid food. In the five, two, and one talent, we recognise the diversity of gifts wherewith we have been entrusted.

He travels, not according to His divine nature, but according to the dispensation of the flesh which He took upon Him. For He who says to His disciples, Lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world, (Mat. 28:20.) is the Only-Begotten God, who is not circumscribed by bodily form. By saying this, we do not disunite Jesus, but attribute its proper qualities to each constituent substance. We may also explain thus, that the Lord travels in a far country with all those who walk by faith and not by sight. And when we are absent from the body with the Lord, then will He also be with us. Observe that the turn of expression is not thus, I am like, or The Son of Man is like, a man travelling into a far country, because He is represented in the parable as travelling, not as the Son of God, but as man.

For it is just as a man about to go abroad called his servants, and handed over to them his goods.

And first indeed let us see why our Lord is likened to a man setting out on a journey — he who is our one Lord, of whom the Apostle says: "but for us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him" — provided, however, that we are ruled by him alone, and hold neither mammon as lord nor any of those lords who, signifying that they are many, the same Apostle mentions when he says: "for just as there are many gods and many lords". Let us therefore first inquire about his journeying, especially because there seems to be something contrary to his journeying in what he himself promises about himself to his disciples, saying: "where two or three have been gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them", likewise this: "behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age", and what the Baptist says about him (showing that he is everywhere) thus: "but in the midst of you stands one whom you do not know; he it is who comes after me". Therefore someone will say: if he stands even in the midst of those who do not know him, if "wherever two or three have been gathered together in" his "name" he is held to be among them, if through all the days of the disciples' life he is with them "until the consummation of the age", how is he set forth in this parable as journeying abroad? But in treating this we ought to take up also that which Paul says about himself: "but I, absent in body yet present in spirit, have already judged, as if present, that when you are gathered together and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, such a one as this be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ". For if the power of Jesus is gathered together with those who are gathered in his name, he does not journey away from his own but is always at hand to them. But if he is always present to all his own, how do his parables introduce him as journeying abroad?

See whether we can resolve in this way the question that is asked. For he who says to his disciples: "behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age", and likewise: "where two or three have been gathered together in my name, there am I also in the midst of them" and the rest, and who stands even in the midst of those who do not know him — he is the only-begotten of God, God the Word and wisdom and righteousness and truth and peace, who is not shut in by any bodily compass. According to this nature of his divinity he does not journey abroad; but he journeys abroad according to the dispensation of the body which he took up, according to which he was both troubled and made sorrowful, saying: "now is my soul troubled", and again: "my soul is sorrowful even unto death". But in saying these things we do not dissolve the man of the body that was assumed, since it is written in John: "every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not of God"; rather, we preserve to each substance its own property. For if every faithful man "who is joined to the Lord is one spirit", how much more is that man, whom Christ took up according to the dispensation of the flesh, not to be dissolved from him nor to be called other than he? And see how he says just as a man about to go abroad; for he was not a man but just as a man, and as though a man he will journey abroad — he who was everywhere according to the nature of his divinity. At the same time consider that the completion of the sentence does not seem to be written thus: just as a man journeying, so also Jesus, or thus: so also I, or thus: so also the son of man; because it is he himself who is set forth in the parable as journeying abroad as though a man. For he is not a man who is "wherever two or three have been gathered together in" his "name", nor is a man with us "all the days until the consummation of the age", nor is it a man that is present to the faithful gathered everywhere, but the divine power that was in Jesus.

We can also say the following about this passage: it is in no way contrary that this same Jesus, according to one understanding, should be everywhere, but according to another should journey abroad. For if we, "while we are in the body, journey abroad away from the Lord (for we walk by faith, not by sight)", then in all who are in the body and journey abroad away from the Lord, the Lord also journeys abroad from them as they walk "by faith", "not by sight". But if we journey abroad "from the body" toward the Lord, then he too will be with us, and in return for the fact that we have walked "by faith", it will come about that afterward we may also walk "by sight". And by "sight" we mean the sight of the Word and of wisdom and of truth and of righteousness and of peace and of everything whatsoever that is the only-begotten of God. And you will understand the sight of the Word and the sight of wisdom when you have understood what the Apostle says: "my children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you". For understanding Christ formed in someone, you will consequently, according to a formation of this kind, see also the sight of Christ. This one, then, who as though a man set out abroad, called his servants, and handed over to them his tested money in chaste utterances — since his "utterances" are "chaste utterances, silver tried by fire, proven, purged seven times".

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q: But see Him everywhere, not requiring it again immediately. For in the case of the vineyard, He let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country; and here He committed to them the talents, and took His journey, that thou mightest learn His long-suffering. And to me He seems to say these things, to intimate the resurrection. But here it is no more a vineyard and husbandmen, but all servants. For not to rulers only, nor to Jews, but to all, doth He address His discourse.
(ubi sup.) Otherwise; The five talents denote the gift of the five senses, that is, the knowledge of things without; the two signify understanding and action, the one talent understanding only.

(ubi sup.) This lesson from this Gospel warns us to consider whether those, who seem to have received more in this world than others, shall not be more severely judged by the Author of the world; the greater the gifts, the greater the reckoning for them. Therefore should every one be humble concerning his talents in proportion as he sees himself tied up with a greater responsibility.

Whenever you see of those who have received from Christ a dispensation of the oracles of God that some have more and some less; that some have not in comparison of the better sort half an understanding of things; that others have still less; you will perceive the difference of those who have all of them received from Christ oracles of God. They to whom five talents were given, and they to whom two, and they to whom one, have divers degrees of capacity, and one could not hold the measure of another; he who received but one having received no mean endowment, for one talent of such a master is a great thing. His proper servants are three, as there are three sorts of those that bear fruit. He that received five talents, is he that is able to raise all the meanings of the Scriptures to their more divine significations; he that has two is he that has been taught carnal doctrine, (for two seems to be a carnal number,) and to the less strong the Master of the household has given one talent.

And to one he gave five talents, but to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own capacity, and he departed. Immediately he who had received the five talents went away and worked with them and gained another five talents. Likewise also he who had received the two gained another two with them. But he who had received the one went away, dug in the earth, and hid his lord's money.

Therefore, if ever you see that, among those who have received from Christ the dispensation of the oracles of God, some indeed possess more and something more divine and more abundant, while others possess less and (so to speak) do not understand even half of the matters at hand in comparison with those who are much better, while still others possess even less — you will observe the differences among those who have received the oracles of God from Christ, since the capacity of those to whom five talents were given was one thing, and that of those to whom two were given was another, and that of those to whom one was given was another, and one did not have the measure of the other. And he who received the one talent received indeed a gift not to be despised; for even one talent of such a lord is a great thing. Yet there are three proper servants of him who went abroad as a man, just as there are also three kinds of those who bear fruit, of whom "some" indeed make "a hundred, some sixty, but some thirty". But there even he who made thirty is saved. Here, however, this discourse condemns him who had received the one talent and hid it in the earth. And I ask whether those who received five talents can be understood as the more perfect who received the more divine and loftier sense of Scripture; and those who received two rose indeed a little above the letter but were not able to ascend to that greatness; and the third ones, who received nothing above the letter which they received at first. Therefore there is, altogether, concerning the numbers in these things which we are discussing, a discourse worthy of such a Lord our Savior — I mean concerning the five and the two and the one.

But we, being of small stature and less able to unfold such things, judge that perhaps those who are able to lead all the perceptible senses of the Scriptures up to the more divine senses (which Solomon calls divine, and which Jeremiah calls the "senses of the heart", and which by Paul in the letter to the Hebrews are called "senses exercised for the discernment of good and also of evil") — these are they who, besides the five talents, gained another five, working with them and by teaching training themselves and raising themselves up to greater knowledge; for having conducted themselves in a saving manner and teaching diligently, they worked and gained another five; for no one easily receives an addition of any virtue other than of that which he has — for example, the wise man grows in wisdom, the faithful man in faith. Or thus: he acquired another five; since each one teaches to another that which he himself knows, and teaches another as much as he himself knows, no more. Therefore whatever anyone has in himself, this he acquires in another by teaching him, making him have what he himself also has. Therefore he who had the five is not said to have acquired more than the five which he had, and he who had the two, no more than the two which he had. But if we ought to speak also of the two talents, we shall speak of those as well: that they who did not remain in the letter, but seeking to ascend by their own understanding above it, yet not being able to arrive above the rank of the aforesaid two, these are they who, from him who knew their capacity, received two talents, having been taught bodily doctrine (for two seems to be the carnal number), and upon these they gained two, that is, a more bodily instruction and another a little loftier than it.

But there was a certain one of the servants gathering to himself a lesser capacity, on account of which the householder gave one talent as to one less able; and the servant, receiving it, having a certain earth, dug, and placed it in its depth, when he ought rather to have sent it up and put it upon the tables. But since three proper servants are reported to belong to that householder, I ask whether they can, after they believed and became his servants, as being capable of trading, afterward have received from the householder his money, so that one indeed both worked and gained, and another gained, but another, through fear not sufficiently faithful, buried and hid his lord's money. And it appears in his very defense, through the things which he says, that he indeed feared the lord (having the fear of God, just as another had "the zeal of God", "but not according to knowledge"), and out of fear hid his talent in the earth. Such are they who neither move nor examine the things that are said, nor give themselves over to the profiting of souls, but wish to keep hidden the things they have received and been entrusted with. If therefore you ever see anyone who has indeed acquired some capacity and has the capacity of speaking and of profiting souls to whatever degree, and hides this capacity (so that he only hands on the bare word which he was entrusted with and received as a deposit committed to him by his lord) and lives in obscurity, unknown to many even to those who have great sins, and does not bring himself forward in the good which he received from God — although he may have a certain religious manner of life not blameworthy to many — do not hesitate to say that such a one is he who received one talent and hid it in the earth.

But if, on account of that which is written, that such a one is sent "into the outer darkness", what is said displeases you — if on account of the fact that someone did not teach he is judged as one who did not use the capacity given to him for the profiting of souls — recall the apostolic saying which says: "for woe is me if I shall not have preached the Gospel".

For not on account of any other blameworthy conduct of his, but on account of this alone, if he shall not have preached the Gospel, does he confess that woe will be to him. For it manifestly appears that that man expected to hear: "wicked and slothful servant", and the rest, unless he had preached the Gospel, although the other things of his life had been upright. For these things and things like these ought especially to be held in mind by those who put "their hand", that is, their action, "to the plow" of teaching the doctrine of Christ, so that, knowing to whom woe is laid up (not on account of anything else except that they do not teach), they may not turn "back" after they have once put "their hand to the plow" that plows the souls of men, so that after this they may also receive the seeds of the word.

But this one who as a man about to go abroad called his servants and handed over to them his goods, "came after much time", after he had sent forth those fit for trading in the salvation of souls. And therefore perhaps it is not easily found that any one of those who were fit for such a work should quickly pass from this life; as is manifest from the fact that even the apostles grew old, of whom he says to Peter: "when you shall have grown old, you shall stretch out your hand", and the rest; and concerning Paul it is said to Philemon, "but now as Paul the aged", though he was a young man when Stephen was being stoned for the testimony of Christ and he himself was guarding the garments of those who were killing him. And this we have said on account of that which he says: after much time the lord of those servants came.

And observe in this place that the servants do not go to the lord, that they may be judged and receive things worthy of their deeds, but the lord comes to them,

when that which was said shall have been fulfilled: "since the time has come". And coming, he will set the account with them concerning all things whatsoever they have done, weighing the gains of good works and the losses of sins, so that, setting the account and diligently examining all things, he may deal with each one as is fitting. We ought therefore — as those who by sinning have incurred loss but by working good things gain — thus with all watchfulness to keep our hearts, so that when our lord shall have come and set the account with us, we may not be found to have incurred loss even for an idle word.

(ubi sup.) There are also some who though they cannot pierce to things inward and mystical, yet for their measure of view of their heavenly country they teach rightly such things as they can, what they have gathered from things without, and while they keep themselves from wantonness of the flesh, and from ambition of earthly things, and from the delights of the things that are seen, they restrain others also from the same by their admonitions.

He that had received five talents, that is, having received his bodily senses, he doubled his knowledge of heavenly things, from the creature understanding the Creator, from earthly unearthly, from temporal the eternal.

Or, They that have their senses exercised by healthy conversation, both raising themselves to higher knowledge and zealous in teaching others, these have gained other five; because no one can easily have increase of any virtues that are not his own, and without he teaches others what he himself knows, and no more.

(ubi sup.) Again, there are some who by their understanding and their actions preach to others, and thence gain as it were a twofold profit in such merchandize. This their preaching bestowed upon both sexes is thus a talent doubled.
Or, gained other two, that is, carnal instruction, and another yet a little higher.
(ubi sup.) To hide one's talent in the earth is to devote the ability we have received to worldly business.

Or, This servant who has received one talent and hid it in the earth is the people that continue in the Law, who through jealousy of the salvation of the Gentiles hide the talent they have received in the earth. For to hide a talent in the earth is to hide the glory of the new preaching through offence at the Passion of His Body. His coming to reckon with them is the assize of the day of judgment.

Or otherwise; When you see one who has the power of teaching, and of benefitting souls, hiding this power, though he may have a certain religiousness of life, doubt not of such an one that he has received one talent and hides it in the earth.
After a long time, because there is a long interval between the Saviour's ascension and His second coming.

And note here that the servants do not come to the Lord to be judged, but the Lord shall come to them when the time shall be accomplished. After a long time, that is, when He has sent forth such as are fitted to bring about the salvation of souls, and perhaps for this reason it is not easy to find one who is quite fit to pass forthwith out of this life, as is manifest from this, that even the Apostles lived to old age; for example, it was said to Peter, When thou shalt be old, thou shall stretch forth thy hand; (John 21:18.) and Paul says to Philemon, Now as Paul the aged.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
And they who bring a return unto Him confess frankly, both what is their own, and what their Master's. And the one saith, Lord, "Thou gavest me five talents;" and the other saith, "two," indicating that from Him they received the source of their gain, and they are very thankful, and reckon all to Him.

What then saith the Master? "Well done, thou good" (for this is goodness to look to one's neighbor) "and faithful servant; thou wast faithful over few things, I will set thee over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy Lord," meaning by this expression all blessedness.
Or, That servant who received five talents is the people of believers under the Law, who beginning with that, doubled their merit by the right obedience of an evangelic faith.
He who had received five talents comes first with boldness before his Lord.

And the one who had received the five talents came forward and presented another five talents, saying: Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five besides. His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord. And the one also who had received the two talents came forward and said: Lord, you gave me two talents; behold, I have gained another two. His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord.

Thus the first came forward as one who had confidence in that he had labored and gained; for that very confidence made him bold, so that he was the first to come to the lord and to make his speech boldly, saying: Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five talents upon them. To him the lord spoke a word desirable to all of us, when our Lord shall have settled the account also with us, saying: Well done, good and faithful servant, the opposite of that word which he said to the third: wicked and slothful servant. Who would not wish, receiving exhortation from this scripture, that he might hear from his lord: faithful, which I judge to be like that which was said of Abraham, that "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him unto righteousness". So also for him who heard from his lord: faithful servant, without doubt his faith was reckoned to him unto righteousness, just as the faith of that very man was reckoned unto righteousness, who was faithful in a little (and all the things of this life are little), so that the whole mystery of the resurrection might be entrusted to him, and the administration of the goods on high.

But let us also see whither this good and faithful servant enters, who was faithful in the little of this life. Enter, he says, into the joy of your lord. For all things there are delightful and all things joys, when those who weep here shall laugh there, and those who mourn in praiseworthy fashion shall receive worthy consolation. But as to what he says (whether in the case of the one who had received five talents, or of this one who had received two): coming forward, understand for me the approach and passage from this world to that one, and see that the lord uttered to the second no other word than the one he uttered to the former, saying: Well done, good and faithful servant, you have been faithful over the little, I will set you over the great. And I ask, since the same things were said to both. Perhaps even the one who had the lesser virtue and exercised the whole of it, as much as he had, according to what was fitting, is to have nothing less with God than the one who was in greater virtue, so that in them may be fulfilled what was said: "He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack". Something of this kind is shown also concerning the commandment of love toward God and toward the neighbor, when it says thus: "You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with your whole strength". For without doubt, when anyone shall have loved God "with his whole heart" "and with his whole soul" "and with his whole strength", he has such a reward of love as the one who had a greater heart, or who has a more eminent soul, or who received greater strength. For this alone is sought, that whatever a man may have from God, he should use the whole of it for the glory of God.
(de Trin. i. 8.) This will be our perfect joy, than which is none greater, to have fruition of that Divine Trinity in whose image we were made.
(Hom. in Ev. ix. 2.) And bringing his talents doubled, he is commended by his Lord, and is sent into eternal happiness.

(ubi sup.) The faithful servant is set over many things, when having overcome the afflictions of corruption, he joys with eternal joy in that heavenly seat. He is then fully admitted to the joy of his Lord, when taken in to that abiding country, and numbered among the companies of Angels, he has such inward joy for this gift, that there is no room for outward sorrow at his corruption.

He says, Thou wast faithful in a few things, because all that we have at present though they seem great and many, yet in comparison of the things to come are little and few.

What greater thing can be given to a faithful servant than to be with his Lord, and to see his Lord's joy?

The servant who of five talents had made ten, and he who of two had made four, are received with equal favour by the Master of the household, who looks not to the largeness of their profit, but to the disposition of their will.

That He says of both these servants that they came, we must understand of their passing out of this world to Him. And observe that the same was said to them both; he that had less capacity, but that which he had, he exercised after such manner as he ought, shall have no whit less with God than he who has a greater capacity; for all that is required is that whatever a man has from God, he should use it all to the glory of God.

Or, the servant to whom two talents were committed is the people of the Gentiles justified by the faith and confession of the Son and of the Father, confessing our Lord Jesus Christ, to be both God and Man, both Spirit and Flesh. These are the two talents committed to this servant. But as the Jewish people doubled by its belief in the Gospel every Sacrament which it had learned in the Law, (i. e. its five talents,) so this people by its use of its two talents merited understanding and working.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78
q:
But not so that other one, but how? "I knew that thou art a hard man, reaping where thou sowedst not, and gathering where thou strawedst not: and I was afraid, and hid thy talent: lo, there thou hast that is thine." What then the Master? "Thou oughtest to have put my money to the exchangers," that is, "thou oughtest to have spoken, to have admonished, to have advised." But are they disobedient? Yet this is nought to thee.

What could be more gentle than this? For men indeed do not so, but him that hath put out the money at usury, even him do they make also responsible to require it again. But He not so; but, Thou oughtest, He saith, to have put it out, and to have committed the requiring of it again to me. And I should have required it with increase; by increase upon the hearing, meaning the showing forth of the works. Thou oughtest to have done that which is easier, and to have left to me what is more difficult.
(Hom. in Ev. ix. 3.) The servant who would not trade with his talent returns to his Lord with words of excuse.

(ubi sup.) But there are many within the Church of whom this servant is a type, who fear to set out on the path of a better life, and yet are not afraid to continue in carnal indolence; they esteem themselves sinners, and therefore tremble to take up the paths of holiness, but fearlessly remain in their own iniquities.

Or, By this servant is understood the Jewish people which continues in the Law, and says I was afraid of thee, as through fear of the old commandments abstaining from the exercise of evangelical liberty; and it says, Lo, there is that is thine, as though it had continued in those things which the Lord commanded, when yet it knew that the fruits of righteousness should be reaped there, where the Law had not been sown, and that there should be gathered from among the Gentiles some who were not scattered of the seed of Abraham.

For truly that which is written, To offer excuses excusing sins (Ps. 141:4.) happened to this servant, so that to slothfulness and idleness was added also the sin of pride. For he who ought to have honestly acknowledged his fault, and to have entreated the Master of the household, on the contrary cavils against him, and avers that he did it with provident design, lest while he sought to make profit he should hazard the capital.

Also, by this which this servant dared to say, Thou, reapest where thou sowedst not, we understand that the Lord accepts the good life of the Gentiles and of the Philosophers.

But he also who had received the one talent came and said: Lord, I know that you are a hard man, and you reap where you have not sown, and you gather where you have not scattered; and being afraid I went away, and hid your talent in the earth: behold, you have what is yours. But his lord answering said to him: You wicked and slothful servant, you knew that I reap where I have not sown, and gather where I have not scattered? You ought therefore to have committed my money to the money-changers, so that at my coming I might have received it back with interest.

It seems to me that this man who received the one talent was indeed among the believers, yet not among those acting with confidence in the faith, but rather wishing to hide themselves and doing everything so as not to be recognized as Christians. But perhaps in other respects too their conduct was not sufficiently blameworthy, and what they received they do indeed keep but do not also add to it, neither do they trade with it nor act confidently in it; and therefore the word in them did not advance to something greater nor gain others. Furthermore, those who are of this sort seem to me to have a fear of God and to think of Him as of one austere and hard and implacable; for the very words of the one answering and saying signify this: I knew that you are hard, and as one who knew that He reaps where He did not sow and gathers where He did not scatter. On which account his lord answering him and rebuking him as a wicked and slothful servant, did not indeed confess Himself to be a hard man, as that man supposed, but consented to his other words, saying to him: You knew that I reap where I have not sown, and gather where I have not scattered?

But how are we to understand that our Lord truly reaps where He did not sow, and gathers where He did not scatter? To me it seems thus in this place: that since the righteous man "sows in the spirit", from which also "he shall reap eternal life". But all things which are sown by another (that is, by a righteous man) and reaped unto eternal life, God reaps; for the righteous man is God's possession, who reaps where He Himself did not sow but that righteous man sowed. Consequently we shall also say this, that since the righteous man "has dispersed, has given to the poor", the Lord will gather into Himself all things whatsoever the righteous man "has dispersed and given to the poor". And reaping the things He did not sow and gathering where He did not scatter, He reckons to Himself and considers to have been conferred upon Himself whatsoever shall have been sown or scattered upon the faithful poor, saying to those who have done well to their neighbors: "Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom which is prepared for you. For I was hungry and you gave me to eat" and the rest.

And because He wishes to reap where He did not sow and to gather where He did not scatter, when He shall not have found it, He will say to those who did not furnish Him something to reap and to gather: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me to eat" and the rest.
